vignette:
He is a 55-year-old European man who comes across as composed at first glance, the kind of counselor who has spent years helping other people sort through fear, grief, and conflict. He is single and lives alone, and he speaks about his work with both pride and exhaustion. He has built a life around being steady for others, but that steadiness has been shaken by what he lived through several years ago, when a man-made disaster tore through the community where he worked.

Before the disaster, his days are structured and familiar. He sees clients in a modest office, walks the same route to lunch, and keeps his personal life private. He has always been someone who manages by staying useful. Colleagues describe him as thoughtful and calm, though he has never been especially open about his own pain. He tends to carry things quietly, telling himself that other people have larger problems. That pattern begins long before the traumatic event, but afterward it becomes a way of surviving.

The disaster unfolds in a sudden, chaotic way, with sirens, shouting, and the sense that the ordinary rules of the world no longer apply. He is not physically injured, but he witnesses enough destruction and panic that the scene feels burned into him. He remembers the sound most vividly-the harsh, mechanical noise of emergency vehicles, the crack of collapsing structures, the cries of people searching for loved ones. In the days that follow, he finds himself moving through the aftermath in a kind of shock, doing what needs to be done because stopping feels impossible. As a counselor, he is expected to be useful, so he keeps working, listens to others, and says little about how deeply affected he is.

At first he believes he will recover if he stays busy. Instead, he begins to notice that his body reacts before his mind can catch up. He startles at loud noises, especially sudden bangs and alarms, and his heart races when he hears distant sirens. He begins checking exits whenever he enters a room, scanning for threats without deciding to do so. He avoids news coverage and anything that might contain images of the disaster, but even small reminders can set off a wave of dread. A smell, a tone of voice, a news headline glimpsed on a screen-these can pull him back into the scene with such force that he feels briefly disoriented, as if the event is happening again.

Sleep becomes unreliable. He lies awake replaying fragments of the day, trying to organize events in a way that will make them less frightening, but the mind keeps returning to the same images. When he does sleep, he has vivid dreams that leave him tense and tired in the morning. He wakes with his jaw clenched and his chest tight, sometimes before dawn, and then sits at the kitchen table with coffee gone cold in front of him, unable to settle into the day. Over time, he notices that he is more irritable with clients and with the few friends he still sees. He becomes impatient with minor disruptions and ashamed of how quickly his temper now flares.

He also grows more distant from people. He has always valued solitude, but now isolation feels less like preference and more like retreat. Invitations are declined. Relationships remain shallow. When someone asks how he is, he offers a professional answer and changes the subject. He does not trust that others could understand what the disaster did to him, and he worries that if he begins talking, the memories will overwhelm him. He feels guilty, too, for surviving when others did not fare as well. That guilt appears in quiet moments, especially when he passes the site of the disaster or hears stories from those who lost homes or family members. He tells himself he should be coping better, given his age and training, but self-criticism has become another habit.

At work, the conflict is especially painful. He is still competent, still able to sit with clients and reflect back their pain, but there are days when his concentration slips. He catches himself drifting during sessions, pulled by intrusive images or by a sudden surge of anxiety that feels out of place and hard to explain. He worries that he is failing in the role that once defined him. He pushes through by relying on routine, but the effort leaves him depleted.

Now, as he speaks about the disaster, he does so carefully, as though approaching something fragile and dangerous. He is more guarded than he used to be, but there are moments when the grief underneath the vigilance becomes visible. He describes feeling as if his life split into a before and after, and he has not yet found a way to join those two selves again. Even so, he keeps showing up-to his office, to his routines, to the small obligations that structure his days-carrying the event with him in ways that remain close to the surface.
